8a35a47ce92540a582188c3153c04ff452c1f316.title: AI Agents vs Business Rules in Decision Automation
8a35a47ce92540a582188c3153c04ff452c1f316.transcript: Both business rules and AI agents are ways to automate a decision. So maybe that's to approve a refund or maybe to flag a transaction. But they go about this in different ways. So my question to you is this, have AI agents superseded business rules or do they both have their place? And what's the difference between these things anyway? Well, let's start with business rules and business rules run in a business rules engine that has logic that a person wrote down explicitly, a person like me. So here's a business rule. We could say, if we have an order that is less than 30 days old and we also have a condition here, which is the item was not marked as a final sale. So if and, and we've got a then, the then is we would actually approve the refund. That is the business rule. And that rule has conditions and an action. Now, an agent doesn't necessarily work from rules that are written down. It works a bit differently because with an agent, you give it a goal and you give it some context of the situation. And you also give it access to some tools that it's allowed to call. And the agent works out the steps itself. So instead of providing rules for handling a refund, it's more like, hey, here's the customer and here's the order policy and here's the customer's order history. Now, you sort it out, Mr. AI agent, it's up to you. So which one should be making the decision? Well, one thing about a rules engine is you get a consistent and predictable answer. It checks against conditions against facts. So if the fact is that an order, let's say, is 12 days old, that's a fact. And if there is a fact that the order was not marked as a final sale, well, then the condition comes from the rule. It's under 30 days. It was not a final sale. Both are true. So the rule resolves as approve this condition, approve the refund. There's not any guesswork here because it's simple Boolean logic. The order is either under 30 days or it is not. And that's what deterministic means. The output is a fixed function of the input and business rules are deterministic. Now, AI agents don't work like this because they are built with large language models. And we know that a large language model predicts next tokens. So given the order and the policy and the goal, the model works out a response from patterns that it's picked up in training and it doesn't necessarily fix on one final answer. It's working from a probability distribution over possible responses and picking from it. So for something like this, approve is still the most likely outcome, but deny as an outcome still has some probability as well. And that makes AI agents probabilistic, whereas the rule engines evaluate a fixed condition. The agent picks from a range of likely answers, which is why you can run the same request twice and get different calls. So that's the split. Rules engine, deterministic, the agent probabilistic. So when to use each one? Well, business rules are used when the decision is well defined, meaning you can define the logic ahead of time. So three fund policies are pretty good example of that. But then so is something like a loan eligibility check or an insurance pricing tier. Anything where the inputs are structured and you already know what the answer should be. And then in regulated work, there's another reason as well. The rule that was processed is by its very definition, also the explanation. A rules engine points at the exact condition that triggered the decision. So that is great for audits. And there's also determinism, which helps with testing. Each branch can be unit tested and it will behave the same way in production. It also runs without a model call. So there is no AI inference cost. So there's lots of advantages here to business rules. Now, AI agents are for when the logic cannot be written down ahead of time because the result all depends upon understanding the context of a situation. Now, the input can be messy or it can be unstructured. Or maybe there's just a case that nobody anticipated. So should a refund actually be approved? If it turns out I sent back my order of dumbbells for being too heavy, which is arguably the point of dumbbells. That sort of thing is the wheelhouse of AI agents judgment. Judging the merits of a reason for a return. And that's not really something that's easily captured in deterministic predefined rules. So look, that's the trade off. A rules engine only handles what was anticipated. It will struggle to handle an input that nobody has a rule for. Whereas an agent will generalize because it's working from patterns instead of a fixed branch. So back to the question we started with, have AI agents superseded business rules? Well, in a lot of real systems, the answer is actually to run the two together. It's just a hybrid approach where you end up using both. So let's fill in this flow with a hybrid solution so we can see what it might look like. So at the top here, we start with the request which has come in. And the first thing in the process flow is we're going to navigate to the rules engines. So we'll come down to here. Now why rules first are not an agent first? Well, because rules are comparatively cheap and they're quick to run. So the rules engine checks the request against the policy and then it will determine an action. Basically what we should do. So the order is 12 days old. It's not a final sale. That would mean it's under the auto-approve limit. And we are going to go down here to the final decision. And that final decision will be to approve that request. That's nice and easy. And if something is clearly outside of the policy, then instead of approving that request, we would decline the request. But that's the decision right there. We're basically done. And most refunds and decisions are going to be clear cut like this. It's only when the rules can't decide that the request instead will go down this pass where it will be escalated. And it's escalated to an AI agent. And there's usually a couple of reasons for that kind of escalation. Now the first is that the data itself is going to need some additional work. So a rule needs clean structured facts to check like an order age or a final sale flag. But plenty of refund requests. They're going to turn up with data that's not all that clean. They're going to have a bunch of unstructured input like a paragraph, a free text, or maybe a picture. Rules engines, they by and large work best with structured data. And the agent can also make use of tools as well. Now it might call a vision model to look at that photo of a defective blender or to query the order system for the customer's purchase history, for example. But the agent will work out which tools the situation calls for and in which order those tools should be called. And it does this without being scripted in advance. So at that point an agent can recommend a decision of its own. But it might not get the final word because its recommendation is then going to go down to a set of deterministic guardrails where it will then be evaluated. So a guardrail might specify where anything the agent green lights above a certain threshold should actually route somewhere else. It should go first of all to this box here, which is human in the loop before the final decision is ultimately reached. If it's under a certain threshold, it can go directly to the decision. So we have the potential to check the agent's judgment with a real person in situations where the stakes are highest. So no, agents have not superseded hard coded business rules, but they can work pretty well.  with them, particularly when the data is messy or when we need judgment, or where tool calling can expand the context. Ultimately, the two together can help make better decisions.

### **Final Meeting Summary: Business Rules vs. AI Agents for Decision Automation**

#### **Key Differences Between Business Rules and AI Agents**
- **Business Rules**
  - **Nature**: Deterministic, rule-based logic (e.g., *"Approve refund if order <30 days and not final sale"*).
  - **Execution**: Handled by a rules engine, ensuring **consistent, predictable outcomes**.
  - **Best Use Cases**:
    - Well-defined, structured decisions (e.g., loan eligibility, insurance pricing, policy-based refunds).
    - Scenarios requiring **auditability, transparency, and testability**.
  - **Advantages**:
    - **Cost-efficient** (no AI inference costs).
    - **Deterministic** (same input always produces the same output).
    - **Easy to explain and audit** (clear decision logic).

- **AI Agents**
  - **Nature**: Probabilistic, goal-driven decision-making using **context, tools, and learned patterns**.
  - **Execution**: Operates independently, determining steps based on **ambiguity and adaptability**.
  - **Best Use Cases**:
    - Unstructured or ambiguous scenarios (e.g., refunds for unusual reasons, nuanced customer requests).
    - Cases requiring **judgment, pattern recognition, or handling messy data** (e.g., free text, images).
  - **Advantages**:
    - **Handles edge cases** where predefined rules fall short.
    - **Adapts to new or unforeseen situations** (e.g., policy exceptions, complex refunds).

#### **Hybrid Decision-Making Approach**
- **Combined System**:
  - **Primary Stage (Business Rules)**:
    - Handles **clear-cut, policy-compliant cases** (e.g., auto-approving refunds within limits).
    - **Efficient and cost-effective** for majority of decisions.
  - **Escalation Stage (AI Agents)**:
    - **Takes over ambiguous or complex cases** (e.g., refunds with unusual justifications, unstructured data).
    - Uses **tools** (e.g., vision models, order system queries) to gather context.
    - **Generates recommendations** checked against **deterministic guardrails** (e.g., high-value refunds, policy violations).
  - **Final Review (Human Oversight)**:
    - **High-stakes decisions** (e.g., large refunds, disputed cases) routed to **human approval**.

#### **Decision Workflow for Refund Requests**
1. **Initial Screening (Business Rules)**
   - **Auto-decline**: Cases clearly outside policy (e.g., refunds >30 days).
   - **Auto-approve**: Cases within policy limits (e.g., refunds <30 days, non-final sale).
2. **Escalation (AI Agent)**
   - **Handles ambiguous cases** (e.g., refunds with unusual reasons, unstructured data like free text or images).
   - **Uses tools** (e.g., vision models to analyze receipts, order system queries for history).
   - **Generates a recommendation** (e.g., approve, deny, or request more info).
3. **Guardrails & Human Review**
   - **Deterministic checks**: Ensures recommendations align with hard-coded rules (e.g., no approvals for policy violations).
   - **High-risk cases**: Escalated to **human agents** for final approval.

#### **Strategic Takeaways**
- **Business rules** remain the **primary decision mechanism** for efficiency and consistency.
- **AI agents** act as **specialized assistants** for edge cases, improving adaptability without sacrificing control.
- **Hybrid systems** optimize **cost, speed, and accuracy** by leveraging the strengths of both approaches.
- **Most decisions (e.g., refunds) are resolved at the rules stage**, while AI handles the remaining **10-20% of complex cases**.

This approach ensures **scalability, fairness, and compliance** while reducing manual review workload.
key_decisions: Here are the key decisions extracted from the meeting transcript:
Business Rules vs. AI Agents**: Decisions can be automated using either business rules (deterministic) or AI agents (probabilistic), each with distinct approaches and use cases.
Business Rules Characteristics**:
Run in a business rules engine with explicitly written logic.
Use structured, predefined conditions and actions (e.g., "if order < 30 days old AND not final sale, THEN approve refund").
Provide consistent, predictable, and deterministic outcomes (Boolean logic).
Ideal for well-defined decisions (e.g., refund policies, loan eligibility, insurance pricing).
Advantages: Audit-friendly (explicit conditions), deterministic (easy to test), no AI inference cost.
AI Agents Characteristics**:
Work from goals, context, and tools rather than explicit rules.
Use large language models to predict responses probabilistically (not fixed).
Handle unstructured/messy data (e.g., free text, images) and judge context-dependent scenarios (e.g., refunds for dumbbells deemed "too heavy").
Generalize to unanticipated cases but lack deterministic guarantees.
Hybrid Approach Decision**:
Rules First**: Use business rules for clear-cut cases (e.g., auto-approve/refuse refunds based on structured data like order age or final sale flag).
Agent Escalation**: Escalate ambiguous or complex cases to AI agents for judgment, especially when:
Data is unstructured (e.g., free text, images).
Additional context/tools are needed (e.g., vision models to analyze photos, querying order history).
Guardrails**: Agent recommendations are evaluated against deterministic guardrails (e.g., thresholds for human review or automatic approval/denial).
Human-in-the-Loop**: High-stakes decisions may require human approval before finalizing.
Conclusion**: AI agents have **not superseded** business rules. Instead, a hybrid approach leveraging both (rules for clarity, agents for judgment) yields better decisions overall.
